title: How to claim mutual fund investments after the investor's death
summary: How to claim mutual fund units after an investor dies: who can claim, papers by value, the 21-day settlement rule, ELSS and tax. Calm, plain steps.
body_markdown:
When an investor dies, their mutual fund units are not sold and not lost. They are transmitted, which means moved into the name of the surviving joint holder, the nominee or the legal heirs, and they stay invested until that person decides to keep or sell them. Once the fund house has all the papers, it must complete the claim within 21 days.


If you are reading this because someone in your family has died, we are sorry. The steps below go in order, one at a time.


## What happens to mutual fund units when an investor dies?


The units stay as they are until a claim moves them. Nothing is sold, and no money is paid out on its own.


Moving the units into a claimant's name is called **transmission** . Until it is done, the units keep rising and falling with the fund's NAV (the price of one unit). A fund house will not accept a redemption request from the claimant while the transmission is still pending.


SEBI's transmission framework of 23 July 2026 has been in force since 22 August 2026. It covers units held by a sole holder, or by all joint holders, who have died. It does not apply where there is a dispute or competing claims. Those go to court.


## Who can claim: joint holder, nominee or legal heir?


Three kinds of person can claim, and which one applies depends on how the folio was set up. A **folio** is the account a fund house keeps in an investor's name.


- **A surviving joint holder.** A joint holder is someone whose name is on the folio with the investor. Application forms allow up to three holders. The fund house must transmit the units to the survivor and may ask for nothing except a copy of the death certificate. No KYC (identity check) papers, no indemnities, no undertakings.
- **A nominee.** This is the person the investor named on the folio to receive the units. The nominee receives them "as trustee on behalf of legal heir(s)" of the investor.
- **The legal heirs.** These are the people who inherit the investor's property. They claim when there is no joint holder and no nominee.


The nominee is the person the fund house pays. The fund house is then fully discharged from its liability. But the nominee holds the units on behalf of the legal heirs, so being named as nominee does not by itself make someone the final owner. A disagreement among heirs is between the heirs, not with the fund house.


Suppose a nominee died before the investor and the nomination was never changed. That nominee's share goes to the surviving nominees in proportion to their shares. When there are several nominees, each may stay in the same folio or open a separate folio for their own holding.


Who claims What they need Extra papers


Surviving joint holder Copy of the death certificate None


Nominee Claim form, verifiable death certificate, copy of the statement of account KYC, and for statement-account units a signature attested by a notary or magistrate


Legal heirs, no nomination Claim form and death certificate Depends on the value, as the next section shows


## What documents do you need to claim?


The papers depend on who is claiming and, for legal heirs, on how much the units are worth. Value means the last available NAV. For units held in a statement account with a fund house, it is counted per fund house.


A **verifiable death certificate** can be any one of these:


- the original
- a copy attested by the nominee, subject to checking against the original
- a copy attested by a notary, a gazetted officer or a Judicial Magistrate First Class
- a certificate with a QR code


**A nominee** also fills in the transmission request form and attaches a copy of the statement of account. For units held in a statement account, the checklist adds a nomination form (or an opt-out form) and a FATCA-CRS declaration. The nominee's signature must be attested by a notary or a Judicial Magistrate First Class, in place of the banker's attestation.


**Legal heirs with no nomination** need more, in steps by value. These figures are for units in a statement account, per fund house:


Value of units Papers


Up to ₹10,000 Request form with an undertaking on plain paper, and a document proving the relationship. Only immediate relatives qualify: parents, spouse, children and parents-in-law.


Above ₹10,000, up to ₹10 lakh The same basics, plus a notarised indemnity bond and a notarised affidavit-cum-NOC from all legal heirs. A notarised family settlement deed is another route.


Above ₹10 lakh The affidavit-cum-NOC from all legal heirs, plus one of the options below.


An **affidavit-cum-NOC** is a sworn statement in which the other heirs say they have no objection.


Above ₹10 lakh, the extra item is one of these:


- a copy of the will, with a notarised indemnity bond
- a legal heirship certificate from a revenue authority of Tehsildar rank or higher, with a notarised indemnity bond
- a succession certificate, letter of administration or court decree


In the middle band, a succession certificate, probate, a letter of administration or a court decree can do the job. It replaces the indemnity bond and the other heirs' NOC.


Probate of the will is no longer a mandatory requirement. For units held in demat, the same bands apply at ₹30,000 and ₹30 lakh per beneficial owner. In the top band, a fund house may ask for more papers, but must record its reasons in writing.


Here is how the bands work for one family. A widow with no nomination on record claims units worth ₹6,00,000 with one fund house and ₹14,00,000 with another, each valued at the last NAV. The first claim falls in the middle band: an indemnity bond and an affidavit-cum-NOC from the other heirs. The second is above ₹10 lakh. She needs the NOC plus a will or a legal heirship certificate, each with a notarised indemnity bond, or a succession certificate. Each fund house must settle within 21 days of complete papers.


## How do you make the claim?


You make one claim with each fund house, or with its registrar, using the common transmission request form. Fund houses must put this form on their own, their registrar's and AMFI's websites, along with a help desk and a transmission webpage.


When you submit the claim, the fund house must acknowledge it. At that moment it must also tell you about any papers that are missing, incomplete or wrong. Some fund houses let you submit the claim online and track it.


Once all the papers are in, the fund house must process the case within 21 calendar days. If it delays or rejects the claim, it must tell you why in writing.

Check one more thing. One fund house's scheme document says units under a loan lien cannot be transmitted until the lender releases the lien. Our guide to[loans against mutual funds](https://koshex.com/blog/get-loan-against-mutual-funds) explains how those loans work.

## Is transmission of units taxed?


No. Receiving units after a death is not taxed. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, a transfer by an individual under a will is outside capital gains tax. Units passing to a nominee, joint holder or heir on a death are not taxed as a sale of the deceased's units.


Tax comes only when the new holder sells. Where an asset passed by will, succession or inheritance, section 73 carries over the previous owner's cost. So the gain is worked out from the original investor's cost. The holding period, which is how long the units have been owned, also counts the original investor's time.


The rates depend on the fund. If equity-oriented fund units are sold with securities transaction tax paid, a short-term gain (on units held for 12 months or less) is taxed at 20%. A long-term gain on such units, held for more than 12 months, is taxed at 12.5% on the amount above ₹1,25,000 in a tax year. For Specified Mutual Fund units acquired on or after 1 April 2023, the gain is taxed at the holder's slab rate, whatever the holding period. A resident's redemption gains carry no TDS (tax deducted at source before money reaches you). IDCW (payouts from a fund's income or gains) paid after transmission is the new holder's income.


### What about ELSS units that are still locked in?


A nominee or legal heir may withdraw ELSS units after one year from allotment, even though the lock-in is normally three years. A **lock-in** is a period during which you cannot sell at all.


Take units allotted on 10 March 2025 whose investor died later that year. Ordinarily they could not be sold before 10 March 2028. The nominee or legal heir could redeem them from 10 March 2026. If they do nothing, the units simply stay invested. Our guide on[what to do when an ELSS lock-in ends](https://koshex.com/blog/your-elss-lock-in-period-is-over-whats-next) covers the usual rules, and the[ELSS funds page](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds/categories/elss-funds) describes the category.


## What happens to SIPs after a death?


Tell the fund house about the death as soon as you can, so that it stops any SIP, STP or SWP running in the folio. A SIP is a fixed amount invested at regular intervals. An STP moves money from one fund to another, and an SWP pays out money from a fund at regular intervals.


One fund's scheme document says an SWP ends on receipt of notice of the investor's death or incapacity. It says an STP ceases once the fund house is told of the death. That is one fund's wording, so do not assume every fund works alike.


A surviving joint holder who wants to end a SIP themselves can follow our guide on[how to stop or pause a SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-stop-or-pause-a-sip) .


## How can you make a claim easier for your family?


An investor can name up to three nominees. If no shares are stated, the units are split equally among them.


For new single-holder folios, a nomination is required unless the investor signs an opt-out form. The opt-out form itself warns that without a nominee, legal heirs may need extra legal or court-issued papers, which can delay the process. Your statement of account shows whether a nominee is registered.


Koshex customers can add, change or check nominees on Koshex. Our guide to[mutual fund nomination](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-nomination) explains how. If there is also a bank deposit to claim, see[how to claim a fixed deposit after death](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-claim-fixed-deposit-after-death) . To look at the funds themselves, start from the[mutual funds](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds) page.
